best_for: Windows developers who need a specific Node.js release, often the current LTS, to match a project or a CI setup.
description:
Node.js is a free runtime that runs JavaScript outside the web browser. It is built to handle many network connections at once without the locks and threads that make other servers hard to write, and it is MIT licensed.

You can write a small web server in about a dozen lines, and the project's own hello world example does just that. HTTP support is built in and designed for streaming, which makes Node.js a good base for web frameworks. When one core is not enough, you can start child processes or use the cluster module to spread the load across all your cores. The Learn section on nodejs.org walks you through the basics, and the API docs cover each release.

points.title: Pick an LTS for real work
points.text: Node.js says production apps should run an LTS line. LTS lines get critical fixes for about 30 months in total. Version 26 (Lithium) is LTS, and 24 and 22 are still supported.

points.title: The schedule changes with 27
points.text: Until 26, only even-numbered versions became LTS and odd ones died after six months. From Node.js 27 every major version goes LTS after six months as Current, following an Alpha phase.

points.title: MSI or zip
points.text: The MSI installs machine-wide for x64 or Arm64 and is the option the project recommends for a system-wide install. The zip runs without installing, which suits several versions side by side.

points.title: Free, MIT licensed
points.text: Node.js costs nothing and is run under the OpenJS Foundation.

points.title: Windows only here
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 34 versions. No Mac or Linux build is listed on this site; nodejs.org offers binaries and installers for those systems.
